decks.title: Spherical Surfaces and Thin Lenses — Part 1: Refraction at a spherical surface and the lens maker’s formula
goals: Derive n₂/v − n₁/u = (n₂ − n₁)/R for a convex surface facing the rarer medium, and use it with the New Cartesian signs
Derive the lens maker’s formula and the thin lens formula for a biconvex lens, and apply them to other lens shapes
Predict how the focal length of a lens changes when it is placed in a liquid

slides.narration: Every lens, from a pair of spectacles to a phone camera, is made of curved glass surfaces. In this part we find where a single curved surface forms an image, then put two surfaces together to get the lens maker’s formula, which links the focal length of a lens to its shape and its glass. Finally we see what happens to a lens when it is dipped in water or another liquid.

slides.heading: Signs for refracting surfaces
slides.body_md: We keep the **New Cartesian** convention from mirrors, with the light drawn travelling from left to right. A spherical refracting surface has a **pole P**, a **centre of curvature C** and a **radius of curvature R**.
bullets: For a surface, **R is positive** when C lies on the side the light is going to (convex towards the incoming light) and negative otherwise.
Results hold for **paraxial** rays: close to the axis and making small angles with it.

rows: Measured from the pole P (or the optical centre O of a lens)
Positive if the centre C lies on the side the light goes to

visual.alt: Table of the New Cartesian signs for refracting surfaces and lenses: distances from the pole, real object negative, real image on the far side positive, radius positive if the centre lies on the outgoing side, converging lens positive focal length

slides.narration: The signs are the ones you used for mirrors. Measure every distance from the pole, positive along the light and negative against it. A real object therefore has a negative u, and a real image formed by refraction, on the far side of the surface, has a positive v. The radius is positive when the centre of curvature lies on the side the light is heading to. All our results assume rays close to the axis.

slides.heading: Setting up the derivation
slides.body_md: A convex surface separates a rarer medium ($n_1$) from a denser one ($n_2$). A ray from O meets the surface at A and bends **towards** the normal CA, crossing the axis at the real image I. Let it make angles $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ with the axis at O, I and C.
bullets: Triangle OAC (exterior angle at A): $i = \alpha + \gamma$.
Triangle AIC (exterior angle at C): $\gamma = r + \beta$, so $r = \gamma - \beta$.
D is the foot of the perpendicular from A; for paraxial rays D is at P.

slides.narration: Take one ray from the object O. It strikes the surface at A, where the normal is the line to the centre of curvature C, and bends towards that normal before crossing the axis at I. Mark the small angles alpha, beta and gamma that the ray, the refracted ray and the normal make with the axis. Two exterior-angle results then link them: i equals alpha plus gamma, and r equals gamma minus beta.

slides.heading: Deriving the refraction formula
slides.body_md:
Snell’s law for small angles: $n_1 i = n_2 r$, so $n_1(\alpha + \gamma) = n_2(\gamma - \beta)$. With D at P, $\alpha \approx \dfrac{AD}{OP}$, $\beta \approx \dfrac{AD}{PI}$, $\gamma \approx \dfrac{AD}{PC}$. Signs: $OP = -u$, $PI = v$, $PC = R$:
$$n_1\left(\dfrac{1}{-u} + \dfrac{1}{R}\right) = n_2\left(\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{v}\right) \;\Rightarrow\; \dfrac{n_2}{v} - \dfrac{n_1}{u} = \dfrac{n_2 - n_1}{R}$$
bullets: Derived here for a convex surface facing the rarer medium with a real image; with signs, the same formula is used for every case.
For a flat surface, $R \to \infty$: $\dfrac{n_2}{v} = \dfrac{n_1}{u}$, the real and apparent depth result.

slides.narration: For small angles Snell’s law becomes n one times i equals n two times r. Substitute the two angle relations, and replace each angle by its tangent: the height of A divided by the distance along the axis. Put in the signs, with u negative, and the height cancels. The result is n two over v minus n one over u equals n two minus n one, all over R. A flat surface gives the apparent depth rule.

slides.heading: The two focal points of a surface
slides.body_md: A single surface has **two** focal lengths. Parallel rays from the left meet at $F_2$ ($u \to -\infty$): $f_2 = \dfrac{n_2 R}{n_2 - n_1}$. An object at $F_1$ gives parallel rays inside ($v \to \infty$): $f_1 = -\dfrac{n_1 R}{n_2 - n_1}$.
bullets: They are unequal: $\dfrac{f_2}{f_1} = -\dfrac{n_2}{n_1}$.
Worked example 1: $f_2 = \dfrac{1.5 \times 6.0}{0.5} = +18$ cm and $f_1 = -12$ cm.

rows: 12 cm in front of the end

slides.narration: A single curved surface has two different focal points. Parallel light coming from the air is brought to a focus inside the glass, at f two, which is n two R over n two minus n one. An object at the first focal point, in front of the surface, sends a parallel beam into the glass. For the glass rod these are eighteen centimetres inside and twelve centimetres in front, in the ratio of the indices.

slides.heading: Thin lenses and the signs of their radii
slides.body_md: A lens has two refracting surfaces. In a **thin** lens the thickness is negligible, so both poles are at the **optical centre O**. With light from the left:
bullets: Biconvex: $R_1 > 0$ (C₁ on the right), $R_2 < 0$ (C₂ on the left).
Biconcave: $R_1 < 0$, $R_2 > 0$. A plane face has $R = \infty$.
Lenses thicker at the centre converge light in air; lenses thinner at the centre diverge it.

slides.narration: A lens is two curved surfaces close together. If its thickness is small compared with the radii and distances, we call it thin and measure everything from its optical centre. For a biconvex lens with light from the left, the first centre of curvature lies to the right, so R one is positive, and the second lies to the left, so R two is negative. A plane face has an infinite radius.

slides.heading: Deriving the lens maker’s formula
slides.body_md:
**Surface 1** (air to glass) alone forms an image $I_1$ at $v_1$: $\dfrac{n}{v_1} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{n - 1}{R_1}$.
**Surface 2** (glass to air) treats $I_1$ as its object (thin lens: same distance $v_1$) and forms the final image I: $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{n}{v_1} = \dfrac{1 - n}{R_2}$.
**Add:** the $n/v_1$ terms cancel:
$$\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = (n - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$$

The rays never reach it, because the second surface bends them again, so I one acts as the object for the second surface, going from glass back into air. Write both equations for a thin lens and add them. The terms in v one cancel, leaving one relation between u, v, the two radii and n.

slides.heading: Lens maker’s formula and thin lens formula
slides.body_md:
For an object at infinity the image is at the **focus**: $u \to -\infty$, $v = f$. So
$$\dfrac{1}{f} = (n - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right) \qquad \text{(lens maker’s formula)}$$
and therefore
$$\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f} \qquad \text{(thin lens formula)}$$
bullets: Turning a thin lens round (R₁ → −R₂, R₂ → −R₁) leaves f unchanged: both foci are the same distance from O.
f depends on the glass (n) and the shape (R₁, R₂), and also on the medium around the lens.

visual.alt: Table of the lens maker’s formula for biconvex, equiconvex, plano-convex and biconcave lenses, with the signs of the radii

slides.narration: If the object is very far away, the rays arrive parallel and meet at the focus, so v becomes f. That gives the lens maker’s formula: one over f equals n minus one, times one over R one minus one over R two. Putting it back, the general equation becomes the thin lens formula, one over v minus one over u equals one over f. Reversing a thin lens does not change its focal length.

slides.body_md: A biconvex lens is ground from glass of $n = 1.6$ with radii 18 cm and 36 cm. Find its focal length (a) with the 18 cm face towards the object, (b) turned round. (c) What is the focal length of a plano-convex lens of the same glass with $R = 18$ cm?

visual.alt: Worked table: the biconvex lens has a focal length of 20 centimetres either way round; the plano-convex lens of the same glass has 30 centimetres

slides.narration: With the more curved face first, R one is plus eighteen and R two is minus thirty six. The bracket is one eighteenth plus one thirty sixth, which is three thirty sixths, and times nought point six gives one twentieth, so f is twenty centimetres. Turned round, the two terms swap but their sum is the same. Flatten one face and the bracket loses a term, so the focal length grows to thirty centimetres.

slides.heading: A lens in a liquid
slides.body_md:
The lens maker’s formula really uses the index of the glass **relative to the surroundings**. A lens of index $n$ in a medium of index $n_m$:
$$\dfrac{1}{f} = \left(\dfrac{n}{n_m} - 1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right) \qquad \dfrac{f_{\text{liquid}}}{f_{\text{air}}} = \dfrac{n - 1}{n/n_m - 1}$$
bullets: $n_m < n$: same kind of lens, but weaker (longer f).
$n_m = n$: no refraction at all; the lens cannot be seen to focus.
$n_m > n$: a convex lens **diverges** light, a concave lens converges it.

functions.label: lens of n = 1.6, f = 20 cm in air

x.label: refractive index of the surrounding liquid

visual.alt: Graph of the focal length of a glass lens of refractive index 1.6, 20 centimetres in air, against the refractive index of the liquid it is placed in: 60 centimetres in water, rising steeply as the liquid index approaches that of the glass, where the lens stops focusing
visual.caption: f(liquid) = f(air) × (n − 1)/(n/n_l − 1).

slides.narration: In the derivation, n was really the index of the glass compared with what surrounds it. In a liquid that ratio is closer to one, so the bending is weaker and the focal length longer. If the liquid has the same index as the glass, the lens does nothing at all. If the liquid is optically denser than the glass, a convex lens becomes a diverging one. The graph shows the focal length shooting up as the liquid index approaches that of the glass.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: the lens under water and in oil
slides.body_md: The lens of worked example 2 ($n = 1.6$, $f = 20$ cm in air) is placed (a) in water ($n = 4/3$), (b) in a liquid of index 1.70. Find its focal length each time.
bullets: (a) $\dfrac{n}{n_w} - 1 = \dfrac{1.6}{4/3} - 1 = 0.2$, against $0.6$ in air: $f_w = 20 \times \dfrac{0.6}{0.2} = 60$ cm (still converging, three times weaker).
(b) $\dfrac{1.6}{1.70} - 1 = -0.0588$: $f = 20 \times \dfrac{0.6}{-0.0588} = -204$ cm: the lens now **diverges** light.

visual.alt: Worked table: the lens has focal length plus 20 centimetres in air, plus 60 in water, and about minus 204 centimetres in a liquid of index 1.70, where it diverges light

slides.narration: In water the glass is only one point two times denser than its surroundings, so the factor n over n m minus one drops from nought point six to nought point two, and the focal length triples to sixty centimetres. In the liquid of index one point seven the factor turns negative, about minus nought point nought six, and the convex lens behaves as a weak diverging lens of focal length about two hundred centimetres.

In this part we measure how strongly a lens bends light, its power in dioptres, and find the size of the images it forms. Then we combine lenses, first touching each other and then separated, and finally send light through a lens to a mirror and back again, following the image step by step.

slides.heading: Images formed by a convex lens
slides.body_md: Use $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$ with $f > 0$. Three easy rays fix the image: parallel to the axis → through $F_2$; through O → undeviated; through $F_1$ → parallel.
bullets: Real images form on the far side ($v > 0$) whenever the object is beyond $F_1$.

visual.alt: Table of images formed by a convex lens for five object positions, from infinity to inside the focus

slides.narration: For a convex lens use the thin lens formula with a positive focal length, or draw three rays. A ray parallel to the axis passes through the far focus; a ray through the optical centre goes straight on; a ray through the near focus comes out parallel. As the object moves in from far away, the real image moves out from the focus and grows, until inside the focus the image becomes virtual.

slides.heading: Magnification of a lens
slides.body_md:
The ray through the optical centre is undeviated, so the triangles ABO and A′B′O are similar:
$$m = \dfrac{h'}{h} = \dfrac{v}{u}$$
(For a mirror $m = -v/u$; for a lens the minus sign is absent because the image forms on the far side.)
bullets: m negative: real and inverted; m positive: virtual and erect.

rows: Virtual, erect image (same side as the object)

visual.alt: Table of what the sign and size of the magnification of a lens mean, and the magnification of a single refracting surface

slides.narration: The ray through the optical centre goes straight through, so the object, its image and the centre form two similar triangles. The ratio of heights is v over u. Unlike a mirror, there is no minus sign. For a real image of a real object, u is negative and v positive, so m is negative and the image is inverted. A virtual image has m positive and is erect.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a magnified real image

bullets: Step 1 — $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{21} - \dfrac{1}{28} = \dfrac{4 - 3}{84}$, so $v = +84$ cm (real, on the far side).
Step 2 — $m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{84}{-28} = -3$; $h' = mh = -6$ cm: **inverted, three times the size**.

slides.heading: Power of a lens
slides.body_md:
The **power** of a lens measures how strongly it converges or diverges light:
$$P = \dfrac{1}{f\text{ (in metres)}} \qquad \text{unit: dioptre (D)} = \text{m}^{-1}$$
bullets: Converging lenses have positive power, diverging lenses negative power.
A shorter focal length means a larger power: the lens bends rays more.
Opticians prescribe lenses by power.

visual.alt: Table of focal lengths and powers: reading glasses plus 2.5 dioptres, a 50 millimetre camera lens plus 20 dioptres, a lens of minus 80 centimetres minus 1.25 dioptres, a hand lens plus 12.5 dioptres

slides.narration: The power of a lens is one over its focal length in metres, measured in dioptres. A converging lens has a positive power and a diverging lens a negative one. The shorter the focal length, the more sharply the lens bends rays, and the larger its power. A fifty millimetre camera lens has a power of twenty dioptres; reading glasses of forty centimetres have plus two and a half.

slides.heading: The thin lens formula as a straight line
slides.body_md: Rewrite the formula as $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{u} + P$ (distances in metres). A graph of $1/v$ against $1/u$ is a straight line of **slope 1**, cutting both axes at a distance P from the origin.
bullets: On the 1/v axis: object at infinity, image at F.
On the 1/u axis: object at F, image at infinity.

points.label: object at F: image at infinity

visual.alt: Straight-line graph of one over v against one over u for a convex lens of power plus 6 dioptres: slope one, meeting the one over v axis at plus 6 and the one over u axis at minus 6; below the one over u axis the image is virtual
visual.caption: Thin lens formula as a straight line: 1/v = 1/u + P.

slides.narration: If you plot one over v against one over u, the thin lens formula becomes a straight line of slope one. It meets the one over v axis at the power: there the object is at infinity and the image at the focus. It meets the one over u axis at minus the power, where the object sits at the focus. Below that axis the image is virtual. This is a quick way to find f from experimental data.

slides.heading: Thin lenses in contact
slides.body_md:
Lens 1 alone forms $I_1$: $\dfrac{1}{v_1} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f_1}$. $I_1$ is the (virtual) object for lens 2, at the same distance since the lenses touch: $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{v_1} = \dfrac{1}{f_2}$. Adding:
$$\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f_1} + \dfrac{1}{f_2} = \dfrac{1}{F} \qquad P = P_1 + P_2$$
bullets: The pair acts as one lens of focal length F; magnification $m = m_1 m_2$.
Combinations are used to build lenses of a chosen power and to reduce colour defects.

slides.narration: Put two thin lenses together. The first lens alone would form an image I one. That image becomes the object for the second lens, and because the lenses touch, its distance is the same v one. Write the two lens equations and add them: v one cancels, and the pair behaves as a single lens whose reciprocal focal length is the sum of the two reciprocals. In other words, powers simply add.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: combining powers
slides.body_md: A lens of power +8.0 D is placed in contact with a lens of power −5.0 D. Find the power and focal length of the combination, and where it images an object 50 cm away.
bullets: Step 2 — $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{F} + \dfrac{1}{u} = 3.0 - 2.0 = 1.0$ m⁻¹, so $v = +1.0$ m (real image 100 cm beyond the pair).

visual.alt: Worked table: plus 8 dioptres and minus 5 dioptres in contact give plus 3 dioptres, a converging combination of focal length 33.3 centimetres

slides.narration: Powers add, so plus eight and minus five give plus three dioptres. The combination converges, with a focal length of one third of a metre, about thirty three centimetres. Working in metres and dioptres, one over v is three minus two, which is one per metre, so the object at fifty centimetres is imaged one metre beyond the pair.

slides.heading: Separated lenses: one image at a time
slides.body_md: When lenses are a distance d apart, find the image step by step:
bullets: If $I_1$ lies beyond lens 2, $u_2 > 0$: a **virtual object** (the rays reach lens 2 still converging).
Measure each distance from the lens being used.

nodes.label: I₁ is the object for lens 2

visual.alt: Flow of the method: find the image of the first lens, use it as the object for the second lens at distance v1 minus d, find the final image, and multiply the magnifications

slides.narration: For lenses some distance apart, work one lens at a time. Find the image formed by the first lens, then treat that image as the object for the second, measuring its distance from the second lens: u two equals v one minus d. If the first image would lie beyond the second lens, u two is positive and we call it a virtual object. The overall magnification is the product of the two.

Light passes through the lens twice; treat each pass separately.

slides.narration: A neat way to find the focal length of a convex lens is to put a plane mirror behind it. Move a pin until its inverted image appears right beside it with no parallax. At that point the pin is at the focus: its light leaves the lens as a parallel beam, the mirror sends the beam straight back, and the lens focuses it again in the same plane. The distance from the pin to the lens is f.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: a lens and a plane mirror
slides.body_md: An object is 18 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 12 cm. A plane mirror is 27 cm behind the lens. Find the final image.
bullets: Pass 1 (lens): $\dfrac{1}{v_1} = \dfrac{1}{12} - \dfrac{1}{18}$, $v_1 = +36$ cm, $m_1 = -2$: $I_1$ would be 9 cm **behind** the mirror.
Mirror: the converging rays are turned back to $I_2$, 9 cm in front of it, i.e. 18 cm from the lens ($m = +1$).
Pass 2 (lens, light now going right to left; measure along it): $u = -18$ cm, $v = +36$ cm, $m_3 = -2$. Final image 36 cm in front of the lens, $m = (-2)(+1)(-2) = +4$: **real and erect**.

slides.narration: First pass: the lens would form an image thirty six centimetres away, but that is nine centimetres beyond the mirror. The mirror turns the converging rays round, so they meet nine centimetres in front of it, eighteen centimetres from the lens. On the way back that point is a real object eighteen centimetres from the lens, which images it thirty six centimetres in front of the lens. Two inversions make the image erect, four times the size.

slides.heading: A lens with a curved mirror
slides.body_md: The same step-by-step method works with a concave or convex mirror behind the lens. A useful special case:
bullets: If the lens’s image $I_1$ falls at the **centre of curvature** of the mirror, the rays meet the mirror normally and retrace their path: the final image forms **on the object itself**, inverted.
Use this to find R of a mirror, or the position of a mirror, from a coincidence of object and image.
A silvered lens (a lens with one face silvered) is not part of the ISC syllabus; here the mirror is always separate.

slides.narration: A curved mirror behind the lens is handled in the same way: lens, then mirror, then lens again. One special case is very useful. If the lens forms its image exactly at the centre of curvature of the mirror, every ray strikes the mirror normally and comes straight back along its own path, so the final image lands on the object itself. Note that we keep the mirror separate from the lens.

slides.narration: To sum up: the thin lens formula and m equals v over u give the position and size of an image, with the signs telling you its nature. Power is one over the focal length in metres. Powers of lenses in contact add. For separated lenses, or a lens with a mirror, find one image at a time, use it as the next object, and multiply the magnifications.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 2
bullets: Lens: m = v/u (no minus sign); mirror: m = −v/u.
Convert f to metres before finding the power; keep its sign.
In the contact derivation, state that I₁ is the object for the second lens at the same distance.
For separated lenses, re-measure distances from the second lens; a positive u₂ means a virtual object.
On the return pass through a lens, measure distances along the returning light.

visual.alt: Table of common questions and the key point for each

slides.narration: Remember that a lens has m equals v over u, with no minus sign. Convert focal lengths to metres before finding power, and keep the sign. In the contact derivation, say that the first image is the object for the second lens. For separated lenses, re-measure every distance from the lens you are using. And on the way back through a lens, measure distances along the returning light.

notes.title: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and Thin Lenses — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Refraction at a single spherical surface
sections.body_md:
- **New Cartesian convention** (light from left to right): distances from the pole P; along the light positive; real object u < 0; R positive when the centre of curvature C lies on the side the light goes to. Paraxial rays only.
- **Derivation (convex surface facing the rarer medium n₁, real image in the denser medium n₂):** a ray from O meets the surface at A and bends towards the normal CA, crossing the axis at I. With α, β, γ the angles at O, I and C: i = α + γ (triangle OAC) and γ = r + β (triangle AIC). Small angles: n₁i = n₂r and α ≈ AD/OP, β ≈ AD/PI, γ ≈ AD/PC with D at P. Putting OP = −u, PI = v, PC = R gives $\dfrac{n_2}{v} - \dfrac{n_1}{u} = \dfrac{n_2 - n_1}{R}$. With signs, the same formula is used for other cases.
- **Focal lengths of a surface:** $f_2 = \dfrac{n_2 R}{n_2 - n_1}$ (parallel light from the first medium), $f_1 = -\dfrac{n_1 R}{n_2 - n_1}$; $f_2/f_1 = -n_2/n_1$.
- **Magnification:** $m = \dfrac{n_1 v}{n_2 u}$. **Flat surface** (R → ∞): $n_2/v = n_1/u$, the real and apparent depth relation. A point at the centre of curvature is seen at its true place (its rays meet the surface normally).

key_terms.definition_md: Rays close to the principal axis, making small angles with it, so that sin θ ≈ tan θ ≈ θ.
Positive when the centre of curvature lies on the side to which the refracted light travels.

sections.heading: 2. Lens maker’s formula, thin lens formula and lenses in liquids
sections.body_md:
- **Thin lens:** two surfaces, thickness negligible; distances from the optical centre O. Light from the left: biconvex R₁ > 0, R₂ < 0; biconcave R₁ < 0, R₂ > 0; a plane face R = ∞.
- **Derivation (biconvex lens in air):** surface 1 alone: $\dfrac{n}{v_1} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{n - 1}{R_1}$. Its image I₁ is the object for surface 2: $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{n}{v_1} = \dfrac{1 - n}{R_2}$. Adding: $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = (n - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$. For u → −∞, v = f: **lens maker’s formula** $\dfrac{1}{f} = (n - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$, hence the **thin lens formula** $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$.
- **Special shapes:** equiconvex f = R/[2(n − 1)]; plano-convex f = R/(n − 1); biconcave f negative. Reversing a lens does not change f.
- **In a medium of index n_m:** replace n by n/n_m: $\dfrac{1}{f} = \left(\dfrac{n}{n_m} - 1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$, so $\dfrac{f_{\text{liquid}}}{f_{\text{air}}} = \dfrac{n - 1}{n/n_m - 1}$. n_m < n: weaker, same type; n_m = n: no focusing; n_m > n: the lens changes type (an air bubble shaped like a convex lens in glass diverges light).

key_terms.definition_md: The point at the centre of a thin lens through which rays pass undeviated.
1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂), linking the focal length of a thin lens to its index and radii.

sections.heading: 3. Magnification and power
sections.body_md:
- **Magnification:** $m = \dfrac{h'}{h} = \dfrac{v}{u}$ (from the undeviated ray through O). m negative: real, inverted; m positive: virtual, erect.
- **Convex lens:** real, inverted images for objects beyond F₁ (at 2F₁ → at 2F₂, same size); virtual, erect, enlarged inside F₁. **Concave lens:** always virtual, erect, diminished, between F₁ and O.
- **Power:** $P = \dfrac{1}{f}$ with f in metres; unit dioptre (D) = m⁻¹. Converging +, diverging −. A shorter focal length means a larger power.
- **Graph:** 1/v = 1/u + P is a straight line of slope 1, meeting both axes at a distance P from the origin.
- **Displacement method:** for fixed object–screen distance D, two lens positions a distance x apart give sharp images; $f = \dfrac{D^2 - x^2}{4D}$ and m₁m₂ = 1.

key_terms.definition_md: The reciprocal of its focal length in metres; measured in dioptres, positive for converging lenses.
The unit of lens power: the power of a lens of focal length one metre (1 D = 1 m⁻¹).

sections.heading: 4. Thin lenses in contact
sections.body_md:
- **Derivation:** lens 1 alone: $\dfrac{1}{v_1} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f_1}$. I₁ is the object for lens 2 at the same distance (lenses touching): $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{v_1} = \dfrac{1}{f_2}$. Adding: $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f_1} + \dfrac{1}{f_2}$, so the pair acts as one lens with $\dfrac{1}{F} = \dfrac{1}{f_1} + \dfrac{1}{f_2}$ and $P = P_1 + P_2$.
- Magnification of the pair: m = m₁m₂. Equal and opposite powers cancel (P = 0, like a parallel-sided plate).
- **Lens on a plane mirror with a liquid:** a liquid layer between a convex lens and a plane mirror forms a plano-concave liquid lens in contact with the glass lens; the pin–image coincidence distance is then the focal length F of the pair, giving the liquid lens from 1/f_liquid = 1/F − 1/f_glass.

sections.heading: 5. Combinations of separated lenses, and a lens with a mirror
sections.body_md:
- **Separated lenses (distance d):** find v₁ for lens 1; the object for lens 2 is at $u_2 = v_1 - d$ (measured from lens 2); if I₁ lies beyond lens 2, u₂ > 0 (**virtual object**: the rays reach lens 2 still converging). Total magnification m = m₁m₂.
- **Lens with a mirror:** light passes the lens, is reflected, and passes the lens again. Treat each step in turn: lens image → object for the mirror (a plane mirror forms its image as far in front as the object is behind) → object for the lens on the return pass, measuring distances along the returning light. m = m₁ × m(mirror) × m₃.
- **Auto-collimation:** a pin at the focus of a convex lens backed by a plane mirror coincides with its own inverted image, whatever the lens–mirror distance: a quick way to measure f.
- **Image back on the object:** if the lens’s image falls at the centre of curvature of a concave or convex mirror placed behind it, the rays retrace their path and the final image forms on the object (inverted). Silvered lenses are not in the ISC syllabus.

key_terms.definition_md: A point towards which rays are converging when they meet a lens or mirror; it lies beyond the element and has u > 0.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Signs first: n₁ is the medium the light comes from; R positive when C is on the outgoing side; real object u < 0.
- Lens: m = v/u (mirror: m = −v/u); P = 1/f with f in metres.
- In a liquid use n/n_m; a liquid denser than the glass reverses the lens.
- Combinations: one image at a time; u₂ = v₁ − d; multiply magnifications; on a return pass measure along the returning light.

cards.front_md: Refraction formula for a spherical surface?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{n_2}{v} - \dfrac{n_1}{u} = \dfrac{n_2 - n_1}{R}$.

cards.front_md: Which medium is n₁ in the surface formula?
cards.back_md: The medium the light comes from (where the object is).

cards.front_md: When is R of a refracting surface positive?
cards.back_md: When its centre of curvature lies on the side the light goes to.

cards.front_md: Exterior-angle results used in the surface derivation?
cards.back_md: i = α + γ and r = γ − β.

cards.front_md: Second focal length of a surface?
Magnification produced by one refracting surface?
cards.back_md: $m = \dfrac{n_1 v}{n_2 u}$.

cards.front_md: Surface formula with R → ∞ gives?
cards.back_md: n₂/v = n₁/u: the real and apparent depth relation.

questions.stem_md: A lamp in air faces the convex end of a long acrylic rod (n = 1.49). The lamp is 40 cm from the end, and the centre of curvature of the end lies 5.0 cm inside the rod. With the light from the lamp taken as travelling from left to right, the values to use in n₂/v − n₁/u = (n₂ − n₁)/R are

options.text_md: u = −40 cm and R = +5.0 cm
u = +40 cm and R = +5.0 cm
u = −40 cm and R = −5.0 cm
u = +40 cm and R = −5.0 cm

questions.solution_md: Distances are measured from the pole. The lamp is on the side the light comes from, so u is negative; the centre of curvature is on the side the light goes to, inside the rod, so R is positive — option (a).

questions.stem_md: One end of a long acrylic-glass rod (n = 1.6) is ground to a convex surface of radius 4.0 cm. A small bright bead in air is 20 cm from this end, on the axis. Find the distance of its image from the end of the rod, in cm, with its sign.

A goldfish swims in a spherical glass bowl of radius 15 cm filled with water (n = 4/3). A child looks at it from outside along a line through the centre of the bowl, and the fish is 10 cm from the near wall. Neglecting the thin glass, find the image distance v of the fish from the wall, in cm, with its sign (light travelling from the fish towards the child).
questions.solution_md: Light goes from water to air: $n_1 = 4/3$, $n_2 = 1$, $u = -10$ cm. The centre of the bowl is on the water side, against the light, so $R = -15$ cm. $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1 - 4/3}{-15} + \dfrac{4/3}{-10} = \dfrac{1}{45} - \dfrac{2}{15} = -\dfrac{5}{45}$, so $v = -9.0$ cm: a virtual image 9.0 cm inside the bowl, slightly nearer than the fish and magnified ($m = \dfrac{n_1 v}{n_2 u} = 1.2$).

marking_scheme.step: Signs: n₁ = 4/3, n₂ = 1, u = −10 cm, R = −15 cm

questions.stem_md: A glass rod (n = 1.5) has a convex end of radius 3.5 cm. A beam of light travelling in air parallel to the axis of the rod enters this end and is brought to a focus ___ cm inside the glass.
questions.solution_md: For $u \to -\infty$: $\dfrac{1.5}{v} = \dfrac{0.5}{3.5}$, so $v = f_2 = \dfrac{n_2 R}{n_2 - n_1} = \dfrac{1.5 \times 3.5}{0.5} = 10.5$ cm.

questions.stem_md: A small bead in air is 6.0 cm from the convex end (radius 5.0 cm) of a thick glass rod of refractive index 1.5. The image of the bead formed by refraction at this end is

options.text_md: real, 22.5 cm inside the glass
virtual, 9.0 cm from the end on the air side
virtual, 22.5 cm from the end on the air side
real, 15 cm inside the glass

questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1.5}{v} = \dfrac{0.5}{5.0} - \dfrac{1}{6.0} = 0.100 - 0.167 = -0.0667$, so $v = -22.5$ cm. The negative sign puts the image on the air side: the rays inside the glass still diverge, so the image is virtual. The bead is nearer than the first focal point (10 cm) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Sunlight falls along the axis onto the convex polished face, of radius of curvature R, of a large glass block of refractive index 1.5. Inside the glass the light converges to a point at a distance from the pole of

options.text_md: 2R
3R

questions.solution_md: For parallel light $u \to -\infty$: $\dfrac{1.5}{v} = \dfrac{0.5}{R}$, so $v = f_2 = \dfrac{n_2 R}{n_2 - n_1} = 3R$. (2R is the first focal length measured in air; R/2 is the focal length of a mirror) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Letting R become infinite in n₂/v − n₁/u = (n₂ − n₁)/R gives the apparent-depth result: a pebble 12 cm below a flat water surface (n = 4/3), viewed from directly above, appears 9.0 cm below the surface.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. With R → ∞, n₂/v = n₁/u. Light goes from water (n₁ = 4/3) to air (n₂ = 1) with u = −12 cm, so v = (n₂/n₁)u = (3/4)(−12) = −9.0 cm: the pebble appears 9.0 cm deep, i.e. real depth ÷ n.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A point object in air on the axis of a convex glass surface always forms a real image inside the glass.

**Reason (R):** A convex glass surface facing the air converges light that enters the glass through it.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true: (n₂ − n₁)/R > 0, so the surface converges light. A is false: an object nearer than the first focal point, |u| < n₁R/(n₂ − n₁), gives a negative v, a virtual image on the air side — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A hemispherical glass paperweight (n = 1.5, radius 7.5 cm) rests with its flat face on a letter printed on a page, the letter directly below the top of the dome. Viewed from above, where does the letter appear? Compare this with a flat glass slab 7.5 cm thick.

answer.model_answer_md: The letter is at the centre of curvature of the dome: $u = -7.5$ cm, $R = -7.5$ cm (glass to air). $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1 - 1.5}{-7.5} + \dfrac{1.5}{-7.5} = -\dfrac{1}{7.5}$, so $v = -7.5$ cm: the letter is seen at its **true position** (its rays meet the dome normally). A slab would raise it by $7.5\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{1.5}\right) = 2.5$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Object at the centre of curvature: no shift; slab shift t(1 − 1/n).

marking_scheme.step: Dome: v = −7.5 cm, letter at its true place

questions.stem_md: A glass marble (n = 1.5) of radius 1.0 cm is held in a beam of sunlight. Treating each surface in turn, find where the light is brought to a focus, measured from the far side of the marble.

answer.model_answer_md:
**First surface** (air to glass, $R_1 = +1.0$ cm, $u \to -\infty$): $\dfrac{1.5}{v_1} = \dfrac{0.5}{1.0}$, so $v_1 = 3.0$ cm from the front, i.e. 1.0 cm beyond the back surface.
**Second surface** (glass to air, $R_2 = -1.0$ cm): the rays still converge towards that point, a **virtual object** at $u_2 = 3.0 - 2.0 = +1.0$ cm.
$\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1 - 1.5}{-1.0} + \dfrac{1.5}{1.0} = 0.5 + 1.5 = 2.0$, so $v = 0.5$ cm: the focus is 0.5 cm beyond the back of the marble.

questions.solution_md: Surface 1 gives v₁ = 3.0 cm; virtual object u₂ = +1.0 cm for surface 2; v = 0.5 cm.

marking_scheme.step: v₁ = 3.0 cm from the front surface
Virtual object u₂ = +1.0 cm, R₂ = −1.0 cm

questions.stem_md: A glass rod (n = 1.5) has a convex end of radius 3.0 cm. A tiny arrow 1.5 mm tall stands upright in air 15 cm from this end, on the axis. Find the position of its image, the magnification, and the height and nature of the image.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\dfrac{1.5}{v} = \dfrac{0.5}{3.0} + \dfrac{1}{-15} = 0.167 - 0.067 = 0.100$, so $v = +15$ cm (inside the rod, real).
For a single surface $m = \dfrac{n_1 v}{n_2 u} = \dfrac{1 \times 15}{1.5 \times (-15)} = -0.667$.
$h' = mh = -0.667 \times 1.5 = -1.0$ mm: a **real, inverted** image 1.0 mm tall, 15 cm inside the rod.

questions.solution_md: Surface formula for v; m = n₁v/(n₂u).

questions.stem_md: At what distance in front of the convex end (radius 4.0 cm) of a glass rod (n = 1.5) must a point object in air be placed so that its real image inside the rod is exactly as far from the end as the object is? Answer in cm.
questions.solution_md: Put $u = -a$ and $v = +a$: $\dfrac{1.5}{a} + \dfrac{1}{a} = \dfrac{0.5}{4.0}$, so $\dfrac{2.5}{a} = 0.125$ and $a = 20$ cm.

questions.stem_md: Show that the two focal lengths of a single spherical refracting surface satisfy f₂/f₁ = −n₂/n₁. Find both for a convex water surface (n = 4/3) of radius 8.0 cm, with light arriving from the air.

answer.model_answer_md:
$u \to -\infty$: $f_2 = \dfrac{n_2 R}{n_2 - n_1}$; $v \to \infty$: $f_1 = -\dfrac{n_1 R}{n_2 - n_1}$; dividing, $\dfrac{f_2}{f_1} = -\dfrac{n_2}{n_1}$.
Here $f_2 = \dfrac{(4/3)(8.0)}{1/3} = +32$ cm and $f_1 = -24$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Put u → −∞, then v → ∞.

marking_scheme.step: Both focal lengths from the formula; ratio −n₂/n₁

questions.stem_md: Light travels from left to right through a thin biconcave lens of glass in air. In the lens maker’s formula, the signs of R₁, R₂ and of the focal length f are

options.text_md: R₁ positive, R₂ negative, f negative
R₁ negative, R₂ positive, f negative
R₁ negative, R₂ positive, f positive
R₁ positive, R₂ negative, f positive

questions.solution_md: The first face is concave towards the light: its centre of curvature lies on the incoming (left) side, so R₁ < 0. The second face’s centre lies on the right, so R₂ > 0. Then 1/R₁ − 1/R₂ < 0 and f < 0: a diverging lens — option (b).

questions.stem_md: An optician must grind a plano-convex lens of focal length 50 cm from glass of refractive index 1.52. What radius of curvature must the curved face have? Answer in cm.
questions.solution_md: With the plane face $R = \infty$: $\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{n - 1}{R}$, so $R = (n - 1)f = 0.52 \times 50 = 26$ cm.

questions.stem_md: A biconvex lens is made of glass of refractive index 1.55, with radii of curvature 22 cm and 33 cm. Find its focal length in air, in cm.

marking_scheme.step: Signs R₁ = +22 cm, R₂ = −33 cm in the lens maker’s formula

questions.stem_md: A symmetrical biconcave lens is made of flint glass (n = 1.65), each face having a radius of curvature of 26 cm. Find its focal length in air, in cm, with its sign.
True or false? Turning a thin plano-convex lens round, so that the light meets its flat face first instead of its curved face, changes its focal length.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Curved face first: R₁ = +R, R₂ = ∞; flat face first: R₁ = ∞, R₂ = −R. In both cases 1/R₁ − 1/R₂ = 1/R, so f = R/(n − 1) is unchanged for a thin lens.

questions.stem_md: A glass lens (n = 1.5) has a focal length of +18 cm in air. A diver uses it under water (n = 4/3). Find its focal length in water, in cm.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{f_w}{f_a} = \dfrac{n - 1}{n/n_w - 1} = \dfrac{0.5}{1.125 - 1} = 4$, so $f_w = 4 \times 18 = 72$ cm (still converging).

questions.stem_md: A biconvex lens of crown glass (n = 1.52) is immersed in carbon disulphide (n = 1.63). In the liquid, the lens

options.text_md: converges light more strongly than in air
still converges light, but with a longer focal length
diverges light, because the glass is optically rarer than the liquid
neither converges nor diverges light, because both media are transparent

questions.solution_md: In the liquid the factor $\dfrac{n}{n_m} - 1 = \dfrac{1.52}{1.63} - 1 \approx -0.067$ is negative, while $\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}$ stays positive, so f is negative: the convex lens now diverges light — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A biconvex glass lens has a longer focal length when it is immersed in water than when it is in air.

**Reason (R):** The refractive index of glass relative to water is smaller than its refractive index relative to air.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: 1/f is proportional to (n/n_m − 1), which is smaller in water (1.5/1.33 − 1 ≈ 0.13) than in air (0.5), so the lens bends light less and f is longer — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A thin air gap shaped like a biconvex lens, trapped inside a block of glass, diverges light that passes through it.

**Reason (R):** In the lens maker’s formula the factor (n_lens/n_surroundings − 1) is negative when the lens material is optically rarer than its surroundings.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: for the air lens n_lens/n_surroundings = 1/1.5, so the factor is −1/3 while (1/R₁ − 1/R₂) > 0; f is negative and the convex-shaped air gap diverges light — option (a).

questions.stem_md: For light travelling from left to right, match each thin lens in Column A with the signs of its radii of curvature in Column B.

options.text_md: Biconvex lens
Biconcave lens
Plano-convex lens with its flat face towards the light
Plano-concave lens with its curved face towards the light

questions.solution_md: A radius is positive when its centre of curvature lies on the outgoing (right) side: biconvex → R₁ > 0, R₂ < 0 (1 → q); biconcave → R₁ < 0, R₂ > 0 (2 → s); plano-convex, flat face first → R₁ infinite, R₂ < 0 (3 → p); plano-concave, curved face first → R₁ < 0, R₂ infinite (4 → r).

questions.stem_md: A biconvex glass lens (n = 1.5) has a focal length of 20 cm in air. When it is immersed in a certain oil, it behaves as a diverging lens of focal length 60 cm. Find the refractive index of the oil, and explain why the lens diverges light in it.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\dfrac{f_l}{f_a} = \dfrac{n - 1}{n/n_l - 1}$ with $f_l = -60$ cm: $\dfrac{-60}{20} = \dfrac{0.5}{1.5/n_l - 1}$, so $\dfrac{1.5}{n_l} - 1 = -\dfrac{1}{6}$.
Then $\dfrac{1.5}{n_l} = \dfrac{5}{6}$ and $n_l = 1.8$.
The oil is optically **denser** than the glass ($1.8 > 1.5$), so $n/n_l - 1 < 0$ and, with $(1/R_1 - 1/R_2) > 0$, f is negative: light bends away from the thicker middle of the lens.

questions.solution_md: f_l/f_a = (n − 1)/(n/n_l − 1) with f_l = −60 cm.

marking_scheme.step: Oil denser than glass makes (n/n_l − 1) negative

questions.stem_md: Using the lens maker’s formula, show that a thin biconcave glass lens in air always diverges light, whatever the radii of its two faces.

answer.model_answer_md: For light from the left, $R_1 = -|R_1|$ and $R_2 = +|R_2|$, so $\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2} = -\left(\dfrac{1}{|R_1|} + \dfrac{1}{|R_2|}\right) < 0$. Glass in air has $n > 1$, so $(n - 1) > 0$. Hence $\dfrac{1}{f} < 0$: **f is negative** for any radii, and the lens is diverging.

questions.solution_md: Both terms of the bracket are negative; (n − 1) > 0.

marking_scheme.step: Signs R₁ < 0, R₂ > 0 make the bracket negative

questions.stem_md: A student says that a glass lens (n = 1.5) of power +6.0 D in air will have a power of +3.0 D when used under water (n = 4/3), “since water halves the bending”. Evaluate the claim.

answer.model_answer_md: The claim is **wrong**. Power is proportional to $(n/n_m - 1)$: in air $0.5$, in water $\dfrac{1.5}{4/3} - 1 = 0.125$, a quarter as much. So the focal length becomes four times as long and the power falls to $\dfrac{6.0}{4} = 1.5$ D, not 3.0 D.

questions.solution_md: Factor (n/n_m − 1) falls from 0.5 to 0.125.

marking_scheme.step: Power +1.5 D, so the claim is wrong

questions.stem_md: A plano-convex lens of glass (n = 1.5) has a curved face of radius 9.0 cm. Find its focal length using the lens maker’s formula, and then use the thin lens formula to find the position, magnification and nature of the image of an object 54 cm in front of it.

answer.model_answer_md:
Lens maker: $R_1 = \infty$, $R_2 = -9.0$ cm: $\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{0.5}{9.0}$, so $f = +18$ cm.
Thin lens: $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{18} - \dfrac{1}{54} = \dfrac{2}{54}$, so $v = +27$ cm.
$m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{27}{-54} = -0.50$: a **real, inverted** image half the size, 27 cm beyond the lens.

questions.solution_md: f = R/(n − 1); then 1/v = 1/f + 1/u; m = v/u.

questions.stem_md: A thin glass lens of refractive index n_g, with radii of curvature R₁ and R₂, is used immersed in a liquid of refractive index n_l. Its focal length f in the liquid is given by

options.text_md: $\dfrac{1}{f} = \left(\dfrac{n_g}{n_l} - 1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$
$\dfrac{1}{f} = (n_g - n_l)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$
$\dfrac{1}{f} = \left(\dfrac{n_l}{n_g} - 1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$
$\dfrac{1}{f} = (n_g - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$

questions.solution_md: At each surface the bending depends on the index of the glass relative to the surrounding liquid, so n in the lens maker’s formula is replaced by n_g/n_l. Option (d) ignores the liquid; option (b) is too large by the factor n_l; option (c) has the ratio upside down — option (a).

questions.stem_md: An optician’s prescription for a pair of reading glasses reads +2.75 D. Find the focal length of each lens, in cm (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $f = \dfrac{1}{P} = \dfrac{1}{2.75}$ m $= 0.3636$ m, i.e. $f = 0.3636 \times 100 = 36.4$ cm (positive: converging).

questions.stem_md: A spectacle lens is marked −2.25 D. It is

options.text_md: a converging lens of focal length 44.4 cm
a diverging lens of focal length 2.25 m
a diverging lens of focal length 44.4 cm
a diverging lens of focal length 4.44 cm

questions.solution_md: $f = \dfrac{1}{P} = \dfrac{1}{-2.25}$ m $= -0.444$ m $= -44.4$ cm; the negative power means a diverging (concave) lens — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A convex lens of focal length 15 cm is used to throw a real image of a lamp filament, three times as large as the filament, onto a screen. How far from the lens must the filament be? Give u in cm, with its sign.
questions.solution_md: Real image: $m = \dfrac{v}{u} = -3$, so $v = -3u$. Then $\dfrac{1}{-3u} - \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{4}{3u} = \dfrac{1}{15}$, giving $u = -20$ cm (and $v = +60$ cm).

questions.stem_md: A slide and a screen are fixed 1.20 m apart. A convex lens placed between them forms a sharp image on the screen three times the size of the slide picture. Find the focal length of the lens, in cm.

marking_scheme.step: u = −30 cm, v = +90 cm from the two conditions

questions.stem_md: A toy is 36 cm in front of a concave lens of focal length 18 cm. The image of the toy is

options.text_md: real and inverted, 12 cm beyond the lens, one third the size of the toy
virtual and erect, 36 cm from the lens on the toy’s side, the same size as the toy
virtual and erect, 18 cm from the lens on the toy’s side, half the size of the toy
virtual and erect, 12 cm from the lens on the toy’s side, one third the size of the toy

questions.stem_md: True or false? A concave glass lens in air cannot form a real image of a real object, wherever the object is placed.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. With f < 0 and u < 0, 1/v = 1/f + 1/u is the sum of two negative terms, so v is always negative: the image is virtual, on the object’s side.

questions.stem_md: The tiny lens of a phone camera has a focal length of 4.0 mm. Its power is ___ dioptres.
An object AB stands on the axis of a thin convex lens and forms a real image A′B′. Using the ray from A through the optical centre O, show that the magnification is m = h′/h = v/u.

answer.model_answer_md: The ray AO passes undeviated through the optical centre to A′. Triangles ABO and A′B′O are **similar** (right angles at B and B′, equal vertical angles at O), so $\dfrac{A'B'}{AB} = \dfrac{OB'}{OB}$. With signs, $A'B' = h'$ (negative), $AB = h$, $OB' = v$, $OB = -u$: $\dfrac{h'}{h} = \dfrac{v}{u}$, so $m = \dfrac{v}{u}$.

questions.solution_md: Similar triangles at the optical centre; then signs.

questions.stem_md: A lamp and a screen are fixed 100 cm apart. A convex lens gives a sharp image on the screen in two positions, 20 cm apart. Find the object and image distances in each position, the focal length of the lens, and the product of the two magnifications.

answer.model_answer_md:
The positions are symmetrical (object and image distances swap): $|u| + v = 100$ and the difference is 20, so position 1: $u = -40$ cm, $v = +60$ cm; position 2: $u = -60$ cm, $v = +40$ cm.
$\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{60} + \dfrac{1}{40} = \dfrac{5}{120}$, so $f = 24$ cm (equivalently $f = \dfrac{D^2 - x^2}{4D}$).
$m_1 = \dfrac{60}{-40} = -1.5$, $m_2 = \dfrac{40}{-60} = -\dfrac{2}{3}$; $m_1 m_2 = 1$.

questions.solution_md: Conjugate positions swap u and v.

questions.stem_md: In a lens experiment a student plots 1/v against 1/u, both in m⁻¹, and gets a straight line that cuts the 1/v axis at +2.5 m⁻¹. The focal length of the lens and the slope of the line are

options.text_md: 40 cm and −1
25 cm and +1
40 cm and +1
2.5 cm and −1

questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{u} + \dfrac{1}{f}$ is a straight line of slope +1 with intercept $\dfrac{1}{f} = P = 2.5$ m⁻¹, so $f = 0.40$ m = 40 cm — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A candle flame 4.0 cm tall is 12 cm in front of a concave lens of focal length 24 cm. Find the height of the image, in cm (3 significant figures).
A convex lens of focal length 60 cm forms an image of the Sun on a sheet of paper. The Sun subtends an angle of 9.3 × 10⁻³ rad at the lens. Find the diameter of the image, in mm.
questions.solution_md: The Sun is effectively at infinity, so its image is in the focal plane. Rays from opposite edges of the disc pass undeviated through the optical centre, so the image diameter is $f\theta = 0.60 \times 9.3 \times 10^{-3}$ m $= 5.58 \times 10^{-3}$ m, i.e. $5.58 \times 10^{-3} \times 1000 = 5.6$ mm.

marking_scheme.step: Image in the focal plane; d = fθ = 5.6 mm

questions.stem_md: A thin lens forms an image of a real object with a magnification of +0.4. The lens and the image are

options.text_md: a convex lens; a real, inverted image smaller than the object
a concave lens; a virtual, erect image smaller than the object
a convex lens; a virtual, erect image smaller than the object
a concave lens; a real, erect image smaller than the object

questions.solution_md: m = v/u > 0 means v has the sign of u: the image is on the object’s side, virtual and erect. A convex lens forms virtual images only when the object is inside F, and they are then enlarged; a diminished virtual image needs a concave lens — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Define the power of a lens and state its SI unit. Find the power of a lens of focal length −16 cm, and say why a lens of shorter focal length is said to be more powerful.

answer.model_answer_md: Power is the reciprocal of the focal length in metres, $P = \dfrac{1}{f}$; its unit is the **dioptre** (D = m⁻¹). Here $P = \dfrac{1}{-0.16} = -6.25$ D (diverging). A shorter focal length bends a parallel beam to a point (or away from one) in a shorter distance: it deviates rays more, so its power is larger.

questions.solution_md: P = 1/f in metres.

marking_scheme.step: P = −6.25 D; shorter f bends rays more

questions.stem_md: Two thin lenses of focal lengths f₁ and f₂ are placed in contact. Derive an expression for the focal length F of the combination, and hence show that the power of the combination is the sum of the powers of the two lenses.

answer.model_answer_md:
Let an object O be at distance u. **Lens 1** alone would form an image $I_1$ at $v_1$: $\dfrac{1}{v_1} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f_1}$.
The light reaches lens 2 before $I_1$ forms, so $I_1$ acts as a (virtual) object for **lens 2**, at the same distance $v_1$ because the lenses touch: $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{v_1} = \dfrac{1}{f_2}$.
Adding: $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f_1} + \dfrac{1}{f_2}$. The pair acts as one lens with $\dfrac{1}{F} = \dfrac{1}{f_1} + \dfrac{1}{f_2}$; with $P = 1/f$, $P = P_1 + P_2$.

questions.solution_md: Image of lens 1 is the object for lens 2; add the two equations.

marking_scheme.step: I₁ as the object for lens 2 at the same distance

questions.stem_md: A converging lens of focal length 16 cm is cemented to a diverging lens of focal length 40 cm. Find the focal length of the combination, in cm (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{F} = \dfrac{1}{16} - \dfrac{1}{40} = \dfrac{5 - 2}{80} = \dfrac{3}{80}$, so $F = 26.7$ cm (power $+3.75$ D, converging).

questions.stem_md: A converging lens of focal length 25 cm is placed in contact with a diverging lens of focal length 25 cm. The combination

options.text_md: is converging, with a focal length of 12.5 cm
is diverging, with a focal length of 50 cm
is converging, with a focal length of 50 cm
has zero power and acts like a parallel-sided glass plate

questions.solution_md: P = +4.0 D − 4.0 D = 0, so 1/F = 0: F is infinite and the pair neither converges nor diverges light — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A camera designer has a converging lens of focal length 12 cm and wants a combination of focal length 20 cm. What focal length must a second thin lens, placed in contact with the first, have? Answer in cm, with its sign.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{f_2} = \dfrac{1}{F} - \dfrac{1}{f_1} = \dfrac{1}{20} - \dfrac{1}{12} = \dfrac{3 - 5}{60} = -\dfrac{1}{30}$, so $f_2 = -30$ cm: a diverging lens.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Two identical converging lenses, each of focal length 30 cm, placed in contact give a combination of focal length 60 cm.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. 1/F = 1/30 + 1/30 = 1/15, so F = 15 cm: the powers add, so the pair is twice as powerful and its focal length is halved.

questions.stem_md: Match each pair of thin lenses placed in contact (Column A, focal lengths given) with the power of the combination in Column B.

options.text_md: +20 cm and +20 cm
+10 cm and −10 cm
+25 cm and −50 cm
−20 cm and −20 cm

questions.stem_md: A converging lens of focal length 15 cm and a diverging lens of focal length 60 cm are held in contact. An object is placed 30 cm in front of the pair. Find the image distance, in cm.

**Assertion (A):** The power of two thin lenses placed in contact is the sum of their separate powers.

**Reason (R):** The magnification produced by two thin lenses in contact is the sum of their separate magnifications.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: 1/F = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂, so P = P₁ + P₂. R is false: the image of the first lens is the object of the second, so the magnifications multiply, m = m₁m₂ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A converging lens of focal length 12 cm is placed in contact with a diverging lens of focal length 10 cm. The combination is

options.text_md: converging, with a focal length of 60 cm
diverging, with a focal length of magnitude 5.5 cm
converging, with a focal length of 22 cm
diverging, with a focal length of magnitude 60 cm

questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{F} = \dfrac{1}{12} - \dfrac{1}{10} = -\dfrac{1}{60}$, so $F = -60$ cm: the diverging lens is the more powerful one, so the pair diverges light — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A magnifying lens of focal length 10 cm is used in contact with a weak converging lens of focal length 40 cm. The focal length of the pair is

options.text_md: 8.0 cm
50 cm
25 cm

questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{F} = \dfrac{1}{10} + \dfrac{1}{40} = \dfrac{5}{40}$, so $F = 8.0$ cm: adding a converging lens shortens the focal length. 50 cm adds the focal lengths instead of their reciprocals — option (a).

questions.stem_md: An optician holds a +9.0 D trial lens in contact with a −3.0 D trial lens. The pair behaves as a single lens of focal length ___ cm.

A student needs a +3.0 D reading lens for a model but has only a +7.0 D lens and a −4.0 D lens. She proposes to tape the two lenses together, face to face. Evaluate her plan, giving the focal length she would obtain.

answer.model_answer_md: The plan **works**. Thin lenses in contact add their powers: $P = +7.0 + (-4.0) = +3.0$ D, a converging combination of focal length $F = \dfrac{1}{3.0}$ m $= 33.3$ cm, as required. The lenses must be thin and touch (on a common axis); any gap would change the result.

questions.solution_md: P = P₁ + P₂ = +3.0 D.

marking_scheme.step: P = +7.0 − 4.0 = +3.0 D, so the plan works
F = 33.3 cm; lenses must be in contact on one axis

questions.stem_md: An equiconvex glass lens rests on a horizontal plane mirror. A pin held above it on the axis coincides with its own image when it is 20 cm above the lens. A little water (n = 4/3) is then placed between the lens and the mirror, and the coincidence position becomes 30 cm. Find the focal length of the water layer, the radius of curvature of the lens faces, and the refractive index of the glass.

answer.model_answer_md:
With a plane mirror, coincidence occurs when the pin is at the focus, so $f_g = 20$ cm and, with water, the glass + water pair has $F = 30$ cm.
The water forms a **plano-concave lens** in contact with the glass: $\dfrac{1}{f_w} = \dfrac{1}{30} - \dfrac{1}{20} = -\dfrac{1}{60}$, so $f_w = -60$ cm.
For the water lens $\dfrac{1}{f_w} = -\dfrac{n_w - 1}{R}$: $R = \dfrac{1}{3} \times 60 = 20$ cm. For the glass, $\dfrac{1}{20} = (n_g - 1)\dfrac{2}{20}$, so $n_g = 1.5$.

questions.solution_md: Coincidence at the focus of the lens (or of the glass + water pair).

marking_scheme.step: R = 20 cm from the plano-concave water lens

questions.stem_md: A parallel beam of light falls on a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. A second convex lens, of focal length 20 cm, is 25 cm beyond the first, on the same axis. Find the position of the final image relative to the second lens: v₂ in cm, with its sign.
questions.solution_md: Lens 1: $v_1 = +10$ cm. For lens 2, $u_2 = 10 - 25 = -15$ cm (a real object 15 cm in front, inside its focal length). $\dfrac{1}{v_2} = \dfrac{1}{20} - \dfrac{1}{15} = -\dfrac{1}{60}$, so $v_2 = -60$ cm: a virtual image 60 cm in front of the second lens.

questions.stem_md: A parallel beam falls on a convex lens of focal length 20 cm. A concave lens of focal length 15 cm is placed 10 cm beyond it, on the same axis. The beam is finally brought to

options.text_md: a real point 10 cm beyond the concave lens
a real point 30 cm beyond the concave lens
a virtual point 6.0 cm in front of the concave lens
a real point 60 cm beyond the concave lens

questions.solution_md: The convex lens alone would focus the beam 20 cm away, 10 cm beyond the concave lens: a **virtual object**, $u_2 = +10$ cm. $\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{15} + \dfrac{1}{10} = \dfrac{1}{30}$, so $v = +30$ cm: a real focus. Taking $u_2 = -10$ cm wrongly gives the 6.0 cm answer — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Two convex lenses, of focal lengths 15 cm and 10 cm, are mounted on a common axis. A parallel beam enters the first lens. For the beam to leave the second lens parallel again, the distance between the lenses must be

options.text_md: 5.0 cm
25 cm
6.0 cm
150 cm

questions.solution_md: The first lens brings the beam to a focus 15 cm beyond it. For the second lens to make it parallel, that point must be at its first focus, 10 cm in front of it: separation 15 + 10 = 25 cm. 6.0 cm is the focal length of the two in contact — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A convex lens of focal length 25 cm stands 10 cm in front of a plane mirror. A pin is moved along the axis on the other side of the lens until the pin and its image coincide with no parallax. The pin is then

options.text_md: 25 cm from the lens
35 cm from the lens
15 cm from the lens
50 cm from the lens

questions.solution_md: Coincidence needs the light to leave the lens as a parallel beam, so that the plane mirror sends it straight back and the lens focuses it again where it started: the pin must be at the focus, 25 cm from the lens, whatever the lens–mirror distance — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? When two lenses some distance apart form a final image, the total magnification is the sum of the magnifications produced by the two lenses.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. The image of the first lens is the object of the second, so the second lens scales an already-scaled image: m = m₁ × m₂ (for example (−2) × (−3) = +6, not −5).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When a pin in front of a convex lens backed by a plane mirror coincides with its own image, the pin is at the focus of the lens.

**Reason (R):** A plane mirror forms a virtual image as far behind it as the object is in front of it.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but R does not explain A. Coincidence happens because light from the focus leaves the lens parallel and the mirror reverses a parallel beam, so the lens refocuses it in the same plane; the image distance rule for a plane mirror is not the reason — option (b).

questions.stem_md: What is meant by a virtual object for the second of two lenses on a common axis? State the sign of its object distance in the New Cartesian convention, and describe one arrangement in which it occurs.

answer.model_answer_md: A virtual object is a point towards which the rays are still **converging** when they reach the second lens: the first lens would form its image beyond the second lens. It lies on the outgoing side, so **u₂ is positive**. Example: a concave lens placed between a convex lens and the point where the convex lens would focus a beam.

questions.solution_md: Rays converging towards a point beyond the lens: u > 0.

marking_scheme.step: Rays converge towards a point beyond the second lens

questions.stem_md: An object is 22.5 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 15 cm. A concave mirror of focal length 10 cm is to be placed on the axis beyond the lens so that every ray returning from the mirror retraces its path. Find the distance between the lens and the mirror, and state where the final image forms and whether it is erect or inverted.

answer.model_answer_md:
Lens: $\dfrac{1}{v_1} = \dfrac{1}{15} - \dfrac{1}{22.5} = \dfrac{1}{45}$, so $I_1$ is 45 cm beyond the lens ($m_1 = -2$).
Rays retrace their paths only if they meet the mirror **normally**, i.e. if $I_1$ is at the mirror’s centre of curvature, $R = 2f = 20$ cm in front of it. So the mirror is $45 + 20 = 65$ cm from the lens.
The mirror images $I_1$ on itself ($m = -1$); the lens then sends the light back to the object position ($m_3 = -0.5$). Total $m = (-2)(-1)(-0.5) = -1$: the final image falls **on the object, inverted**, same size.

questions.solution_md: I₁ at the centre of curvature of the mirror.

marking_scheme.step: Mirror 65 cm from the lens (I₁ at its centre of curvature)
Final image on the object, inverted, same size

questions.stem_md: A convex lens of focal length 12 cm and a concave lens of focal length 18 cm are on a common axis, 6.0 cm apart. An object is 36 cm in front of the convex lens. Find the position of the final image and the total magnification, and state the nature of the image.

answer.model_answer_md:
Convex lens: $\dfrac{1}{v_1} = \dfrac{1}{12} - \dfrac{1}{36} = \dfrac{1}{18}$, $v_1 = +18$ cm, $m_1 = -0.5$.
$I_1$ is $18 - 6.0 = 12$ cm **beyond** the concave lens: a virtual object, $u_2 = +12$ cm. $\dfrac{1}{v_2} = -\dfrac{1}{18} + \dfrac{1}{12} = \dfrac{1}{36}$, so $v_2 = +36$ cm and $m_2 = \dfrac{36}{12} = 3$.
Final image 36 cm beyond the concave lens; $m = m_1 m_2 = -1.5$: **real, inverted**, 1.5 times the size of the object.

questions.solution_md: u₂ = v₁ − d = +12 cm (virtual object).

marking_scheme.step: Virtual object u₂ = +12 cm; v₂ = +36 cm

questions.stem_md: An object is 15 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. A plane mirror stands 22 cm behind the lens, facing it. Light passes through the lens, is reflected, and passes through the lens again. How far from the lens is the final image? Answer in cm.
questions.solution_md: Lens: $v_1 = \dfrac{1}{1/10 - 1/15} = +30$ cm, 8.0 cm behind the mirror. The mirror turns the converging rays back to a point 8.0 cm in front of it, $22 - 8 = 14$ cm from the lens. Return pass (measured along the returning light): $u = -14$ cm, $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{14} = \dfrac{4}{140}$, so $v = 35$ cm: a real image 35 cm from the lens on the object’s side ($m = +5$).

marking_scheme.step: v₁ = 30 cm; mirror image 14 cm from the lens
Return pass: final image 35 cm from the lens

questions.stem_md: (a) A convex spherical surface of radius R separates a rarer medium of refractive index n₁ from a denser medium of refractive index n₂. With a ray diagram described in words, derive the relation n₂/v − n₁/u = (n₂ − n₁)/R for a point object in the rarer medium forming a real image in the denser medium. [3] (b) A long glass rod (n = 1.5) has a convex end of radius 2.5 cm. (i) Find the position of the image of a point object in air 10 cm from the end. (ii) Where must the object be placed for the light inside the rod to travel parallel to its axis? [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) O is the object on the axis, P the pole, C the centre of curvature. A ray OA meets the surface at A and bends towards the normal CA, meeting the axis at I. Let the ray, the normal and the refracted ray make angles $\alpha$, $\gamma$, $\beta$ with the axis; AD is perpendicular to the axis.
Exterior angles: in triangle OAC, $i = \alpha + \gamma$; in triangle AIC, $\gamma = r + \beta$, so $r = \gamma - \beta$. Snell’s law for small angles: $n_1 i = n_2 r$, so $n_1(\alpha + \gamma) = n_2(\gamma - \beta)$.
Paraxial rays (D at P): $\alpha = \dfrac{AD}{OP}$, $\beta = \dfrac{AD}{PI}$, $\gamma = \dfrac{AD}{PC}$, with $OP = -u$, $PI = v$, $PC = R$. Then $n_1\left(-\dfrac{1}{u} + \dfrac{1}{R}\right) = n_2\left(\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{v}\right)$, i.e. $\dfrac{n_2}{v} - \dfrac{n_1}{u} = \dfrac{n_2 - n_1}{R}$.

(b)(i) $\dfrac{1.5}{v} = \dfrac{0.5}{2.5} - \dfrac{1}{10} = 0.10$, so $v = +15$ cm (real, inside the rod).
(ii) Parallel rays inside need $v \to \infty$: $-\dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{0.5}{2.5}$, so $u = -5.0$ cm: the object at the first focal point, 5.0 cm in front of the end.

questions.solution_md: Exterior angles, small-angle Snell’s law, signs; then the formula with v → ∞.

marking_scheme.step: Diagram: O, A, C, I with α, β, γ; i = α + γ and r = γ − β
n₁i = n₂r with α, β, γ as AD/OP, AD/PI, AD/PC
Signs substituted to give the relation

questions.stem_md: (a) Using the relation for refraction at a single spherical surface, derive the lens maker’s formula for a thin biconvex lens of refractive index n in air, and hence the thin lens formula 1/v − 1/u = 1/f. [3] (b) An equiconvex lens of glass (n = 1.5) has a focal length of 15 cm in air. Find (i) the radius of curvature of its faces, (ii) its focal length when immersed in a liquid of refractive index 1.25. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Let a point object O be at distance u from the thin lens (radii $R_1$, $R_2$). **First surface** (air to glass) alone forms an image $I_1$: $\dfrac{n}{v_1} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{n - 1}{R_1}$.
Before $I_1$ forms, the rays meet the **second surface** (glass to air); $I_1$ is its object, at distance $v_1$ (thin lens): $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{n}{v_1} = \dfrac{1 - n}{R_2}$.
Adding: $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = (n - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$. For $u \to -\infty$, $v = f$: $\dfrac{1}{f} = (n - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$, so $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$.

(b)(i) $R_1 = R$, $R_2 = -R$: $\dfrac{1}{15} = 0.5 \times \dfrac{2}{R}$, so $R = 15$ cm.
(ii) $\dfrac{1}{f_l} = \left(\dfrac{1.5}{1.25} - 1\right)\dfrac{2}{15} = 0.2 \times \dfrac{2}{15}$, so $f_l = 37.5$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Surface formula twice, I₁ as the object for surface 2; then u → −∞.

marking_scheme.step: Second surface with I₁ as object; adding the equations
u → −∞ gives the lens maker’s formula and 1/v − 1/u = 1/f

questions.stem_md: (a) Two thin lenses of focal lengths f₁ and f₂ are in contact. Show that they act as a single lens of focal length F given by 1/F = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂. [2] (b) A convex lens of focal length 15 cm is placed in contact with a concave lens. The pair forms a real image of an object 40 cm away on a screen 120 cm from the lenses. Find the focal length of the combination and of the concave lens. [2] (c) Find the power of the combination and say whether it converges or diverges light. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Lens 1 alone: $\dfrac{1}{v_1} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f_1}$. Its image $I_1$ is the object for lens 2, at the same distance $v_1$ since the lenses touch: $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{v_1} = \dfrac{1}{f_2}$. Adding: $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f_1} + \dfrac{1}{f_2}$, which is the thin lens formula for one lens with $\dfrac{1}{F} = \dfrac{1}{f_1} + \dfrac{1}{f_2}$.

(b) $u = -40$ cm, $v = +120$ cm: $\dfrac{1}{F} = \dfrac{1}{120} + \dfrac{1}{40} = \dfrac{4}{120}$, so $F = +30$ cm. Then $\dfrac{1}{f_2} = \dfrac{1}{30} - \dfrac{1}{15} = -\dfrac{1}{30}$, so $f_2 = -30$ cm.

(c) $P = \dfrac{1}{0.30} = +3.33$ D: positive, so the combination **converges** light.

questions.solution_md: Add the two lens equations; then 1/F = 1/v − 1/u and 1/f₂ = 1/F − 1/f₁.

marking_scheme.step: Lens 1 equation and I₁ as the object of lens 2

questions.stem_md: (a) Explain how the final image formed by two thin lenses on a common axis, some distance apart, is found, and how the total magnification is obtained. [1] (b) Two convex lenses of focal lengths 12 cm and 8.0 cm are placed 60 cm apart on a common axis. An object 3.0 cm tall stands 18 cm in front of the first lens. Find the position of the image formed by each lens. [2] (c) Find the size and nature of the final image. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Find the image formed by the first lens; it acts as the object for the second lens, at a distance $u_2 = v_1 - d$ from it. The final image is found with the thin lens formula for lens 2, and $m = m_1 m_2$.

(b) Lens 1: $\dfrac{1}{v_1} = \dfrac{1}{12} - \dfrac{1}{18} = \dfrac{1}{36}$, $v_1 = +36$ cm. Lens 2: $u_2 = 36 - 60 = -24$ cm; $\dfrac{1}{v_2} = \dfrac{1}{8.0} - \dfrac{1}{24} = \dfrac{2}{24}$, $v_2 = +12$ cm beyond the second lens.

(c) $m_1 = \dfrac{36}{-18} = -2$, $m_2 = \dfrac{12}{-24} = -0.5$, $m = m_1 m_2 = +1$. The final image is **real** (v₂ > 0), **erect** and the same size, 3.0 cm tall.

questions.solution_md: u₂ = v₁ − d; m = m₁m₂.

marking_scheme.step: Image of lens 1 is the object of lens 2; m = m₁m₂

questions.stem_md: (a) Describe how the focal length of a convex lens can be found with a plane mirror and a pin, and explain why the pin coincides with its image only when it is at the focus. [2] (b) An object is 30 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 20 cm. A convex mirror is placed on the axis 40 cm behind the lens, and the final image is found to coincide with the object. Find the radius of curvature of the mirror, and state whether the final image is erect or inverted. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Lay the lens on (or in front of) a plane mirror and move a pin along the axis until its inverted image is seen tip to tip with it, with no parallax; the pin-to-lens distance is f. From a pin at the focus, light leaves the lens as a **parallel beam**; the mirror reflects a parallel beam as a parallel beam, so on its return the lens focuses it in the same focal plane. At any other position the returning beam is not parallel and the image forms elsewhere.

(b) Lens: $\dfrac{1}{v_1} = \dfrac{1}{20} - \dfrac{1}{30} = \dfrac{1}{60}$, so $I_1$ would be 60 cm beyond the lens, 20 cm **behind** the convex mirror. The image falls back on the object only if the rays retrace their path, i.e. strike the mirror normally: they must be heading for its **centre of curvature**. So $R = 60 - 40 = 20$ cm.
Magnifications: lens $m_1 = -2$, mirror (rays retrace) $-1$, lens on return $-0.5$: $m = -1$, so the final image is **inverted** and the same size.

questions.solution_md: Parallel beam from F; rays retrace when aimed at the mirror’s centre of curvature.

marking_scheme.step: Method: pin–image coincidence without parallax; distance = f
Reason: parallel beam out and back
I₁ at the mirror’s centre of curvature: R = 20 cm
